title: Duals and supertraces for finite complexes realized in condensed coefficients
statement:
Let $\ell$ be prime, let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of positive prime characteristic $p\ne\ell$, put $s=\operatorname{Spec}k$, and let $E/\mathbf Q_\ell$ be a finite extension inside $\Omega=\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell$ [def-weil-l-adic-numbers, def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension, def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Let $\underline\Omega=\operatorname{Profinite.padicAlgClRingObj}(\ell)$ be the finite-subextension-valued condensed ring of [sk-def-sfb-qlbar-condensed], and put $U_s=p_s^*\underline\Omega$, the tensor unit of $\mathcal D_s=D^b_c(s)[[\underline\Omega]]$ [sk-def-sfb-pulled-back-coefficients, sk-def-sfb-bounded-constructible, def-sfb-dc-tensor]. Use the scalar inclusion $E\to\Omega$ and its pulled-back coefficient map [def-sfb-subfield-to-qlbar-coefficient-map]. On a bounded finite-dimensional $E$-complex, define $\rho_{E,s}$ by replacing each term $E^r$, after choosing a basis, by $U_s^{\oplus r}$, and replacing each differential or chain map matrix by the same matrix acting through $E\to\Omega$. Use total tensor products and Koszul symmetry. This construction is independent of bases up to its canonical change-of-basis isomorphisms, sends quasi-isomorphisms to isomorphisms, and defines an exact strong symmetric monoidal functor
$$\rho_{E,s}:D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E)\longrightarrow\mathcal D_s,$$
where $D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E)$ has the meaning of [def-weil-point-fd-complexes]. It identifies $\rho_{E,s}(E[0])$ with $U_s$ and satisfies $H^i\rho_{E,s}(C)\cong\rho_{E,s}(H^i(C)[0])$. The latter cohomology module evaluated at the geometric point has underlying vector space $H^i(C)\otimes_E\Omega$.

For every $C\in D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E)$, $\rho_{E,s}(C)$ has a right dual in $\mathcal D_s$, given by $\rho_{E,s}(R\operatorname{Hom}_E(C,E))$. Evaluation, coevaluation and the triangle identities are those of the signed finite-free dual complex, interpreted as internal $U_s$-module maps. For every isomorphism $w:P\xrightarrow{\sim}\rho_{E,s}(C)$ in $\mathcal D_s$ and maps $v:P\to P$, $f:C\to C$ such that $w\circ v=\rho_{E,s}(f)\circ w$, $P$ has a right dual and the categorical trace [sk-d-trace] satisfies
$$\operatorname{tr}_{\mathcal D_s}(v)=\epsilon_E\left(\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}_E(H^i(f)\mid H^i(C))\right)\quad\text{in }\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal D_s}(U_s),$$
where $\epsilon_E:E\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal D_s}(U_s)$ sends $a$ to multiplication by its image in $\Omega$, and is an injective ring homomorphism. In particular $U_s$ has a right dual and $\operatorname{tr}(1_{U_s})=\epsilon_E(1)$. Ordinary traces here are those of [def-weil-endomorphism-trace].

proof.text: Put $U=U_s$. On $s=\operatorname{Spec}k$, the profinite-site identification of [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-field-proetale-evaluation] identifies $p_s^*$ with the identity and terminal evaluation with evaluation at the singleton. By the section formula of [sk-def-sfb-qlbar-condensed], $U(s)=\Omega$: every singleton-valued function lies in a finite subextension. The inclusion of [def-sfb-subfield-to-qlbar-coefficient-map] therefore gives scalar multiplication maps $m_a:U\to U$ for $a\in E$, with $m_{a+b}=m_a+m_b$, $m_{ab}=m_a m_b$ and $m_1=1$. These equalities remain true on $U[0]$ in the derived category. If $m_a$ is zero there, its $H^0$ is zero, so its terminal evaluation sends $1$ to $0$. But that value is the image of $a$ in $\Omega$, whence $a=0$. Thus $\epsilon_E(a)=Q(m_a)$ is an injective unital ring homomorphism. This uses evaluation only to test these scalar maps, and makes no conservativity claim for all condensed objects.

proof.text: For finite-dimensional $E$-spaces with chosen bases, send $E^r$ to $U^r$ and a matrix $A=(a_{ij})$ to $(m_{a_{ij}})$. Matrix multiplication and addition are preserved by the ring laws of step 1. If basis changes in source and target are $B$ and $D$, the new matrix is $D^{-1}AB$ and the comparisons are the matrices $B,D$ interpreted over $U$; their naturality is the identity $D(D^{-1}AB)=AB$. For three bases these comparisons compose because matrix multiplication does, so they are canonical change-of-basis isomorphisms. Apply this additive construction degreewise to bounded complexes. It preserves $d^2=0$, chain maps and the chain homotopy equation $f-g=dh+hd$, entry by entry.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text: The cohomological domain in [def-weil-point-fd-complexes] really is covered by bounded finite-dimensional complexes. Given any complex $M$ representing an object of that domain, put $B^i=\operatorname{im}d^{i-1}$ and $Z^i=\ker d^i$. Every $E$-space is projective by [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-projective]. The lifting property in [def-weil-pbc-projective-module] splits $Z^i\twoheadrightarrow H^i(M)$ and $M^i\twoheadrightarrow B^{i+1}$. Thus $M^i=B^i\oplus H_i\oplus L^i$, with $d:L^i\xrightarrow{\sim}B^{i+1}$. Inclusion of the zero-differential complex $(H_i)$ into $M$ induces the identity on cohomology and is a quasi-isomorphism. Its source is bounded finite-dimensional by hypothesis. By [lem-pc-ring-derived-map-representative], morphisms between bounded finite-dimensional complexes in $D(E)$ are exactly chain maps modulo chain homotopy: their terms are projective and the complexes are bounded above. Hence this homotopy category embeds fully faithfully with essential image precisely $D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E)$.

source.place: Tag 064B, lemma-morphisms-from-projective-complex; explicit field splitting to identify the essential image

proof.text: If $q$ is a quasi-isomorphism between bounded finite-dimensional complexes, it is invertible in $D(E)$. Fullness in step 3 represents its inverse by a chain map $r$, and faithfulness says that $rq$ and $qr$ are chain homotopic to the identities. Step 2 sends these two homotopy equations to homotopy equations over $U$. Their images become identities in the derived category [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], so the image of $q$ is invertible. The degreewise matrix construction therefore gives a functor on the homotopy category, hence, through the fully faithful essentially surjective identification in step 3, a functor on the specified full subcategory $D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E)$. Choosing another representative gives the isomorphism obtained by applying the functor to the unique corresponding derived isomorphism; compositions agree by the same full faithfulness. In particular this descent is a functor and respects all the basis comparisons of step 2.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text: For a bounded finite-dimensional complex $C$, apply [lem-wf-bounded-free-complex-projective-cohomology-splitting] over $E$; its projective-cohomology hypothesis follows from [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-projective]. Its explicit complex decomposition into $H^i(C)[-i]$ and identity two-term complexes remains such a decomposition after step 2. The latter summands are contractible after realization, so $H^i(\rho C)$ is the finite free module realizing $H^i(C)$. Equivalently, put this module in degree zero to obtain $H^i(\rho C)[0]\cong\rho(H^i(C)[0])$. This comparison is natural: a linear splitting of kernels and images identifies each cohomology quotient with its chosen complement, and for a chain map the induced map on that quotient is exactly its block from the source cohomology complement to the target one; changing complements changes these descriptions by the quotient identifications. A finite free $U^r$ is finitely presented, using the presentation $U^0\to U^r\xrightarrow{1}U^r$, and hence locally finitely presented on the identity cover. The one-stratum stratification of $s$ then proves constructibility. Thus $\rho C$ belongs to $\mathcal D_s$ and the construction of step 4 lands in that full subcategory.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text: The cohomology module just identified evaluates to $\Omega^r$, where $r=\dim_E H^i(C)$, by [lem-weil-pbc-geometric-field-proetale-evaluation]. More intrinsically its identification with $H^i(C)\otimes_E\Omega$ sends $x\otimes b$ to the vector with coordinates $b x_j$ in any basis of $H^i(C)$. This respects the relation $(a x)\otimes b=x\otimes ab$; the inverse sends $(b_j)$ to $\sum_j e_j\otimes b_j$. The two formulas are inverse, commute with linear maps, and change by the same change-of-basis matrix. This proves the stated geometric evaluation without identifying the entire condensed module category with vector spaces.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text: For $C,D$, each realized term is finite free and therefore flat by [lem-weil-pbc-condensed-finite-free-tensor-exact], applied to the identity cover. Use the exact symmetric monoidal equivalence [lem-pe-internal-section-tensor-comparison] to pass to ordinary sheaf modules; [lem-pc-bounded-above-flat-kflat-site] makes their bounded complexes K-flat, and the same equivalence reflects K-flatness. Thus the relative derived tensor in [sk-def-sfb-derived-tensor-hom] is computed here by the ordinary total tensor. The map $U^r\otimes_U U^t\xrightarrow{\sim}U^{rt}$ sends the pair of basis labels $(a,b)$ to that same label; its inverse is the sum of their tensor inclusions. These maps commute with the differentials $d\otimes1+(-1)^i1\otimes d$, since their entries are the same scalar matrices. They identify $\rho(C\otimes_E D)$ with $\rho C\otimes_U^{\mathrm L}\rho D$, and $\rho(E[0])$ with $U[0]$. Associativity and unit coherence fix every tuple of basis labels; both symmetry maps exchange $(a,b)$ with $(b,a)$ with the same sign $(-1)^{ij}$. Hence these comparisons give a strong symmetric monoidal structure, inherited in the full subcategory with tensor [def-sfb-dc-tensor].

source.place: Tag 06YQ, lemma-bounded-flat-K-flat; finite-biproduct tensor calculation transported by the existing internal/section equivalence

proof.text: The functor commutes with shifts: degree $i$ of $C[1]$ and of $(\rho C)[1]$ is the realization of $C^{i+1}$, and both differentials are the negative of its realized differential. It also preserves the cone of a chain map $f$: it takes the differential matrix $\begin{pmatrix}d_D&f\\0&-d_C\end{pmatrix}$ on $D^i\oplus C^{i+1}$ to that identical matrix over $U$, and preserves the inclusion and projection maps of the cone triangle. By the definition of distinguished triangles in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], every distinguished triangle is isomorphic to a cone triangle; step 3 represents its morphism by a chain map between bounded finite-dimensional complexes. Its cone is still bounded finite-dimensional, and step 5 puts its realization in $\mathcal D_s$. Consequently $\rho$ is exact with the indicated shift comparison.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text: For a bounded finite-dimensional representative $C$, [lem-trf-chain-supertrace], applied to the ordinary ring $E$, gives its dual $C^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_E^\bullet(C,E[0])$, with $(C^\vee)^j=\operatorname{Hom}_E(C^{-j},E)$ and $d^\vee\phi=(-1)^{j+1}\phi d$. It represents $R\operatorname{Hom}_E(C,E)$ as asserted there for perfect complexes. Its evaluation has entries $\phi(x)$ and its coevaluation is $1\mapsto\sum_{i,a}e_{i,a}\otimes e_{i,a}^\vee$; that cited statement supplies the chain-map and both triangle identities. Apply the functor and tensor/unit comparisons of step 7 to these maps and equalities. Functoriality preserves the equalities, and coherence identifies their composites with the two triangle composites for $\rho C$ and $\rho(C^\vee)$. Their matrices are precisely the same signed finite-free dual matrices acting internally over $U$. The dual lies in $\mathcal D_s$ by step 5. This establishes the asserted right dual, including the specified evaluation and coevaluation, without applying an ordinary-ring theorem directly to internal module objects.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text: Represent $f:C\to C$ by a chain map on a bounded finite-dimensional representative, using [lem-pc-ring-derived-map-representative]. Write its trace composite as in [sk-d-trace]. Substituting the evaluation and coevaluation of step 9 and the symmetry of step 7, the composite is $\sum_{i,a}(-1)^{i(-i)}m_{(f^i)_{aa}}=\epsilon_E(\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}_E(f^i))$: coevaluation selects $(e_{i,a},e_{i,a}^\vee)$, the chain endomorphism supplies its $a$th diagonal entry after evaluation, and $(-1)^{-i^2}=(-1)^i$. The matrix trace is [def-weil-endomorphism-trace]. Over the ordinary field $E$, [lem-trf-chain-supertrace] identifies the sum with the ordinary categorical trace, and clause (4) of [prop-trf-trace-formal-laws] identifies that scalar with $\sum_i(-1)^i\operatorname{Tr}_E(H^i(f)\mid H^i(C))$. Only these ordinary-field assertions are used from those two nodes. The internal trace formula follows, as an equality of actual endomorphisms of $U$, from the displayed matrix calculation and step 1.

source.place: First sentence, finite determinant factors: explicit coefficient-point comparison argument

proof.text:
Finally write $R=\rho C$ and $D=\rho(C^\vee)$. For $w:P\xrightarrow{\sim}R$, give $P$ the dual $D$ with $\eta_P=(w^{-1}\otimes1_D)\eta_R$ and $e_P=e_R(1_D\otimes w)$. The two triangle identities follow from [lem-trf-exact-pairing-iso-transport], taking its $U=R$, $V=P$, $E=D$ and its isomorphisms $w^{-1}$ and $1_D$. Naturality of symmetry and $w v=\rho(f) w$ give, directly in the composite of [sk-d-trace],
$$e_P\,c_{P,D}(v\otimes1_D)\eta_P=e_R\,c_{R,D}((wvw^{-1})\otimes1_D)\eta_R=e_R\,c_{R,D}(\rho(f)\otimes1_D)\eta_R.$$
Thus $\operatorname{tr}(v)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(f))$, so step 10 proves the desired formula. Set $C=E[0]$ and $f=1$ to obtain the stated dual of $U$ and $\operatorname{tr}(1_U)=\epsilon_E(1)$.
